Don't do that — bridging the thermal fuse with wire isn't a safe workaround.

That fuse exists specifically to cut power before the fan motor overheats to a dangerous point. It blew because the motor was already running hot, whether from worn bearings, a failing run capacitor, or a short somewhere in the circuit. Jumping it with copper wire doesn't fix any of that — it just removes the one thing stopping the motor from cooking itself. You'd be looking at melted windings, ignition of nearby insulation or debris, or broader damage to the unit, and none of that is worth the risk even for a few hours a day.

The real fix is replacing the failed part — the motor itself, or the whole fan assembly — and figuring out why it overheated in the first place so it doesn't happen again. In the meantime, leave the unit off at the breaker so it doesn't cause more damage while it's waiting on the tech. If you want to get seen sooner, you can check for earlier openings through our in-app scheduling tab.

Happy birthday to your son — the PowerSeeker 70AZ is a great little scope for getting started, and sharing an eclipse together is a great way to break it in.

Quick heads up before you hit buy, though: **don't get that eyepiece-threaded solar filter.** Skip it.

Yes, physically, the 1.25" threads would screw right onto the eyepieces that came with your scope. But that's exactly the problem. The objective lens up front is concentrating all of that intense sunlight into a tight beam by the time it reaches the eyepiece, and the little filter sitting there gets hit with a huge amount of concentrated heat. It can crack or shatter without warning, and if that happens while someone's eye is right up against it, you're looking at permanent eye damage or blindness in an instant.

The filter has to go on the *front* of the telescope — over the objective lens — so the sunlight is dimmed down before it ever enters the tube. What you want is a full-aperture solar filter sized for the 70mm opening on your scope, ideally one marked ISO 12312-2 certified, made for 70mm refractors.

Happy to help you track down the right front-aperture filter for the 70AZ if you want — just say the word so you and your son can watch the eclipse safely.

Here's how I'd tackle sealing those hairline cracks before winter hits, using stuff that's cheap and easy to find.

**Resin/epoxy pick (under $15):**

Grab Loctite Marine Epoxy or J-B Weld ClearWeld — both run $6–$9 at Home Depot or Lowe's. One trick for getting the viscosity down: sit the mixed epoxy in a warm water bath for a minute, or warm the rim area slightly with a hairdryer on low before you apply it. Warming it up lets it flow much thinner so it actually wicks into those hairline fractures via capillary action instead of just sitting on top.

If you want to skip the heating step entirely, thin (water-thin) CA glue — the super glue hobby shops sell for $5–$8 — works great too. It's basically zero viscosity out of the bottle and wicks into micro-cracks instantly.

**Skip the clamps — brush it on instead:**

Don't rig up C-clamps or wood blocks. Carbon rims are hollow structural shells, and squeezing them with localized clamping pressure risks cracking the profile further or pushing the resin back out of the cracks you're trying to fill. Brushing and letting capillary action do the work is the right call here:

1. Wipe down the area around the eyelets with 90%+ isopropyl alcohol to get rid of brake dust, oil, and grime, then let it dry completely.
2. Dab a small amount of your thinned epoxy or thin CA glue right onto the cracks.
3. Give it a minute to wick in on its own — flexing the spoke gently by hand can help pull it deeper into the micro-gaps.
4. Before it fully sets, wipe off the excess with an alcohol-dampened, lint-free rag so it ends up flush with the rim surface rather than sitting in a raised blob.
5. Let it cure fully — 24 hours for standard epoxy — and if you're left with any ridges, wet-sand them down with 800–1000 grit paper.

That should get you a sealed, flush surface that keeps the salt and slush out of the weave this winter.

Alright, let's get you set up for a clean demo and an invisible ceiling patch.

**Tools & floor protection for the demo**

- Reciprocating saw (Sawzall) with bi-metal demo blades — you'll need this to cut through the nails at the plates
- Heavy duty flat pry bar plus a molding bar
- 3 lb mini sledge or a framing hammer
- Scrap 2x4 blocks to use as a fulcrum under your pry bar — keeps you from denting the floor
- Ram Board or 1/8" hardboard taped down over the hardwood with painter's tape for protection
- Eye protection, heavy gloves, N95 mask

Tip for pulling the studs without wrecking anything: cut each stud roughly in half horizontally with the recip saw, then pull both halves inward toward the room. That releases the tension and lets the nails pull straight out of the plates instead of you having to fight the bottom plate down into the hardwood. For the bottom plate itself, slide a thin pry bar between it and the floor, always resting on a scrap block rather than the wood directly — or run a metal-cutting blade under it to flush-cut the nails holding it down.

**Making the ceiling transition disappear**

Materials:
- Drywall matching your existing thickness (1/2" or 5/8")
- 1-1/4" drywall screws
- Paper tape or fiberglass mesh tape
- Setting-type compound (Easy Sand 45 or 90) for the first coat
- Lightweight all-purpose compound for the finish coats
- 6", 10", and 12" taping knives
- Fine sanding sponge or pole sander, 150–220 grit
- PVA primer and flat ceiling paint

Steps:
1. Make sure you've got solid backing along both edges of the gap — add 2x4 blocking flat across the joists if you need something to screw the new patch and the existing drywall edges into.
2. Cut drywall to fit the gap and screw it off every 8–12", sinking the heads just below the surface without blowing through the paper.
3. Bevel the cut edges slightly with a utility knife (a V-groove) and fill flush with the setting compound.
4. Bed paper or mesh tape into wet or fresh compound over the seams and smooth it down with a 6" knife.
5. This is the part that actually makes it disappear: lay down 2–3 thin coats of lightweight compound, going wider each time, moving up to the 10" and then 12" knife, and feathering the edges out 10–12 inches from the seam so there's no ridge to catch the light.
6. Once it's dry, sand it smooth and check your work with a work light held flat against the ceiling — that's the only real way to catch shadows or high spots.
7. Prime with PVA, then paint. If you want it truly seamless in an open floor plan, repaint the whole ceiling corner-to-corner with a dead-flat ceiling paint so there's no sheen mismatch under natural light.

Go with heavy-duty ratchet straps over bungee cords. Bungees have give, and that stretch is exactly what lets a strong gust rock or lift the boxes — which breaks the propolis seal and increases your tipping risk. Ratchet straps hold the whole stack rigid, which is what you want.

**Hardware specs I'd use:**
- **Material:** 100% polyester webbing — it holds up against UV, water, and stretch far better than nylon.
- **Width:** 1 inch. A 2-inch strap is overkill and just harder to thread through iron slats.
- **Rating:** 400–500 lb working load limit (1,200–1,500 lb break strength).
- **Fittings:** Stainless or zinc-plated ratchets with vinyl-coated S-hooks, so nothing scratches the iron or starts rusting on you.

**How I'd secure it, step by step:**

1. **Give it some grip underneath.** Put a rubber mat or non-slip pads under the bottom board — metal-on-wood has almost no friction on its own, and this stops lateral sliding in gusts.

2. **Protect the outer cover.** Add corner protectors or scrap pieces of 1x2 wood on the top edges of the telescoping cover, so the tightened strap doesn't crush the wood or dent the roof.

3. **Anchor and run the straps.** Hook one end under the *structural* iron bars of the landing — not the thin decorative grating. Run the strap up over the center of the outer cover, then hook the other end to the iron on the opposite side.

4. **Tension it down.** Ratchet until the whole hive feels like one solid unit — no wobble at all when you push on it. Zip-tie any slack so it's not flapping around near the entrance.

*Optional:* if you're in and out of the hive a lot and don't want to undo the main strap every time, run one strap just for the bottom board to the landing, and a second, separate strap around the boxes and lid.

Let's go through how the SportDOG 425X actually works, how to introduce it properly, and how to manage things safely before Thanksgiving.

**Setting up the collar and finding a baseline**
The 425X is built as a communication tool for reinforcing known commands — not as a device for instant-correcting vocalizations. A few basics:

- Fit: receiver high on the neck, just below the ears, contact points against skin. You should be able to slide one finger under the strap.
- Acclimation: let him wear it turned off for a few hours a day over 3–5 days so he doesn't learn to associate the collar itself with getting corrected.
- Finding the working level: start at Level 1 on the low range, tap the continuous button, and watch him. You're looking for the lowest level that gets a slight recognition response — a blink, an ear flick, a head turn. Not a yelp, not panic. That low working level is what you'd eventually use to reinforce cues like sit or place — not to deliver a hard correction.

**Why growling and e-collars don't mix the way you're picturing**
Trying to punish a growl on a 5-day timeline is genuinely risky, especially with kids in the house:

- A growl is his early-warning system — it tells you he's uncomfortable, threatened, or guarding something (in this case, his bed). If you shock that warning away, you haven't touched the underlying discomfort, you've just removed his way of telling you about it. Dogs that get punished for growling often stop growling and go straight to biting instead.
- There's also a real risk of him linking the pain to the wrong thing. If he's mid-growl at a child and gets zapped, he may associate the shock with the child rather than with his own behavior — which can make him more defensive around kids, not less.

**What I'd actually do before Thursday**
Given that five days isn't enough to safely work through space-guarding or properly condition a collar, the more reliable move is management, not correction:

1. **Full separation during the gathering.** Set up a quiet room — bedroom, exercise pen, wherever — away from where the four kids will be running around. Give him his bed, water, and something to chew on (frozen Kong, etc.), and keep the door shut or gated so no one wanders in on him.
2. **Bed and space boundaries.** When he's out in shared space, keep his bed tucked in a low-traffic corner nobody has to pass. Make it a hard rule: no kids near him while he's resting or eating.
3. **Save the collar work for after the holiday.** Use it to build a solid "place" or "go to mat" cue in a low-distraction setting, pairing low-level stim with positive reinforcement. Once that's reliable, you can redirect him away from tense situations before they build, instead of reacting after the fact.

Given that this involves a child's safety, I'd strongly encourage working with a certified trainer (CPDT-KA or IAABC) to guide you through this properly rather than handling it solo on a tight deadline.

Okay, deep breath — this is fixable, spider mites are annoying but very treatable. Here's the fastest, safest way to attack this tonight.

First: don't put that 91% alcohol on the leaves at full strength. It'll chemically scorch both the fiddle leaf fig and the monstera.

**Step 1 — Dilute it.** Mix 1 part of the 91% isopropyl with 4 parts warm water, plus a couple drops of mild dish soap, in a bowl or spray bottle. That's plenty strong to kill mites on contact without wrecking the leaf cuticle.

**Step 2 — Shower them first.** Carry both plants to the shower or tub and give every leaf, top and bottom, plus the stems, a good lukewarm rinse. Two minutes of steady spray will physically knock off most of the webbing, mites, and eggs before you even touch a cotton pad — huge time-saver.

**Step 3 — Wipe top to bottom.** Work from the top of the plant downward, and from the stem out toward the leaf tip, so you're not dragging mites back onto spots you've already cleaned. Soak your cotton pads in the diluted solution and get the tops *and especially the undersides* of every leaf, along the veins and where the leaf meets the stem — that's where they love to hide. Change pads often so you're not just smearing mites from leaf to leaf.

**Step 4 — Rinse or not?** You don't have to rinse the diluted mix off, but for extra safety let it sit 10–15 minutes, then wipe or mist with plain water. Keep the plants out of direct sun while they dry so you don't get leaf spotting.

**Step 5 — The part that takes patience.** No single treatment kills eggs that haven't hatched yet, so you won't fully wipe this out tonight in one pass. Plan to repeat the shower-and-wipe routine every 4–5 days for the next 2–3 weeks, checking closely each time.

You caught this early and you're doing all the right things — your monstera and fiddle leaf are resilient and should pull through just fine.

Congrats on wrapping up the wheel throwing class — and what a haul, a 50lb box of red earthenware plus a stash of Mayco Stoneware glazes (the mattes really do look great) is a solid start.

Before you punch anything into that controller, though, there's a compatibility snag worth flagging first:

**Temperature mismatch, in short:**
- Standard red earthenware is a low-fire body — it wants Cone 06–04, roughly 1828–1945°F. Push it to Cone 6 (~2232°F) and it will overfire: bloating, slumping, possibly melting right into the shelf.
- Mayco Stoneware glazes, on the other hand, are made for mid-fire, Cone 5–6.

So the two things you bought don't actually belong in the same firing.

**What I'd do with what you've got:**
1. Fire the earthenware mugs and planters to Cone 04, where they belong. Pair them with low-fire (Cone 06/05) glazes, or leave the planters bare for that classic terracotta look.
2. Hang onto the Mayco Stoneware glazes for a future batch made with an actual Cone 6 stoneware body — they'll shine there.

Now, onto schedules for the KM-1027:

**Bisque profile for your red earthenware (Cone 04):**
- Segment 1: 150°F/hr up to 250°F (slow preheat, lets residual moisture escape)
- Segment 2: 250°F/hr up to 1000°F
- Segment 3: 180°F/hr up to 1150°F (quartz inversion — go easy here)
- Segment 4: 300°F/hr up to 1800°F
- Segment 5: 120°F/hr up to 1945°F (Cone 04) — hold 10 minutes

**Cone 6 glaze profile with drop-and-hold (for mid-fire clay paired with the Mayco glazes):**
If you do go the mid-fire stoneware route down the line, here's a schedule built to minimize pinholing and bring out a smooth matte surface:
- Segment 1: 150°F/hr to 250°F — hold 0 min
- Segment 2: 400°F/hr to 1950°F — hold 0 min
- Segment 3: 120°F/hr to 2232°F (Cone 6) — hold 10 minutes
- Segment 4 (drop and soak): full-speed drop to 2150°F — hold 30 minutes, to let trapped gases heal over
- Segment 5 (controlled cool): 150°F/hr down to 1400°F — hold 0 min, then let the kiln cool naturally from there

One more note: a proper two-step bisque-then-glaze firing is still the more reliable path to a pinhole-free surface — the drop-and-hold segment above is a workaround, not a replacement for it.

Blasting the tabletop directly with a 1500W heater from two feet away isn't the move, even though warming things up in general will help the cure. That kind of concentrated heat tends to make the top layer of oil skin over while it's still wet underneath, so you end up with wrinkling or blistering — and it's also enough heat to warp the wood if it's close and sustained.

Here's what'll actually get you closer to a usable table by Saturday:

1. **Heat the room, not the surface.** Pull the heater back and just let it bring the whole room up to somewhere around 70–75°F, rather than pointing it at the wood.
2. **Get air moving.** Linseed oil cures by oxidation — it needs to react with oxygen, not just dry out — so a box fan or oscillating fan on low, circulating air across the tabletop, will do more for you than heat alone.
3. **Skip the fourth coat tomorrow.** If this coat is still tacky, putting fresh oil on top of it will just seal in the uncured layer underneath, and you'll end up with a gummy mess that can take weeks to sort out. Three coats on oak is already plenty.
4. **Buff it down if it's still tacky later.** After several hours of warm air and circulation, if there's still unabsorbed oil sitting on the surface, take a clean dry cotton rag and buff it off firmly.

Stick with warm ambient air plus steady airflow and that's your best shot at a table that's actually dry and ready to use Saturday night.

Okay, let's get those skips and loops sorted — here's what to dial in plus a couple of tricks for those thick corners.

**Settings to try:**
* **Stitch length:** Push it up to 3.5–4.0, toward the top of your dial. Heavy fabric plus thick upholstery thread needs the extra length so the feed dogs can actually move the layers instead of the thread bunching up on itself.
* **Upper tension:** Bump it to 5–7 (you're probably sitting around 4 now). Looping underneath is a classic sign the top thread isn't being pulled tight enough for the weight of the fabric and thread, so cranking the upper tension up should even things out.

**For getting through the thick corners:**
* **Level out the presser foot ("hump jumper" trick):** Skipped stitches at the transitions usually happen because the front of the foot rides up onto the thick fold and loses downward pressure. Slide a folded scrap of canvas or a bit of cardboard under the *back* of the foot so it stays level as it climbs onto the hem.
* **Hand-crank through the thick spot:** Turn the handwheel toward you manually through that dense 6-layer intersection instead of running the pedal. It gives the needle time to fully punch through and catch the bobbin loop without deflecting.
* **Trim the bulk:** If you haven't already, clip the inner corner folds at 45 degrees inside the double hem to cut down how many layers of canvas and lining are stacked right at that intersection.

Congrats on getting the Skutt fired up! A firing log is exactly the right move for staying sane through glaze testing. Here's a layout you can drop straight into Excel, plus the cost math worked out.

### Kiln Log Table

Columns across the top:

| Col A | Col B | Col C | Col D | Col E | Col F | Col G | Col H | Col I |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Date** | **Firing Type** | **Target Cone** | **Total Time (hrs)** | **Top Shelf** | **Mid Shelf** | **Bottom Shelf** | **Est. Cost ($)** | **Notes / Results** |
| 2023-10-24 | Bisque | Cone 04 | 9.5 | Tile Set A | Tile Set B | Cone pack | *[Formula]* | Good melt, even heat |

### The Electricity Cost

First, the kiln's max draw:

$$\text{240V} \times \text{48A} = 11{,}520\text{ W} = 11.52\text{ kW}$$

For your 9.5-hour ramp (low 3 hrs, medium 3 hrs, high 3.5 hrs), broken out by stage:

* **Low (3 hrs @ ~33% power):** $3 \times (11.52 \times 0.33) \approx 11.40\text{ kWh}$
* **Medium (3 hrs @ ~66% power):** $3 \times (11.52 \times 0.66) \approx 22.81\text{ kWh}$
* **High (3.5 hrs @ 100% power):** $3.5 \times 11.52 = 40.32\text{ kWh}$
* **Total:** $\approx 74.53\text{ kWh}$

At $0.16/kWh, that run cost:

$$74.53 \times 0.16 \approx \mathbf{\$11.92}$$

### Formulas for the Sheet

Drop one of these in **H2**:

* **Average-power version** (assumes a typical ~65% of max power averaged over the whole run):
  `=(D2 * (11.52 * 0.65)) * 0.16`

* **Max-power version** (if you want to assume elements ran at 100% the entire time):
  `=D2 * 11.52 * 0.16`

Tip: swap the `0.16` for a reference to a rate cell like `$J$1` so you can update it easily if your off-peak rate changes. And for the full specs on the kiln itself, the product manual is worth a look.

Happy firing!

Quick but important flag first: capping actively fermenting cider in regular glass beer bottles is a real bottle-bomb risk. Yeast activity doesn't behave on a schedule, and the pressure can build past what those bottles are rated for — cold storage slows things down, it doesn't reliably stop it. So I'm not going to hand you a countdown for that method. Here's what I'd actually do instead to get you sweet cider for Saturday.

**Option A — Sweet still cider (simplest path)**
- Wednesday/Thursday: cold-crash the whole fermenter in the fridge. That drops the yeast out of suspension and halts fermentation while there's still residual sugar left.
- Saturday: rack the cold, clear cider straight into a pitcher or keg to serve. It'll be flat rather than bubbly, but it's safe and it'll still taste good.

**Option B — Sweet *and* sparkling, the traditional way**
Heads up that a week is a tight window for this route, but it's the safe version of what you're picturing:
1. Let the Nottingham finish out completely — you want a stable gravity around 1.000.
2. Back-sweeten with something the yeast can't touch — erythritol, xylitol, stevia, that sort of non-fermentable sweetener.
3. Add a measured dose of priming sugar (or carb drops) to bring it up to a safe carbonation level.
4. Cap and let the bottles condition at room temp for 10–14 days, then chill before serving.

If you've got any kind of keg/draft setup, there's actually a much faster legit option: cold-crash, stabilize with potassium sorbate/metabisulfite, back-sweeten with fresh apple juice, and force-carbonate with CO2 — that can get you there in 24–48 hours. * Felt polishing bobs/wheels

**Progression:**

4. **Fine pre-polish (3000 grit):** Even, consistent passes to get the surface ready for the optical polish stage.

Here's how I'd size and construct a winter fleece sleep sack for a 3-month-old, plus the machine settings to keep everything feeding smoothly.

**Pattern dimensions (0–3 / 3-month size)**

These already build in a 1/2-inch seam allowance:

- Total length: 24–26 inches, shoulder to bottom hem
- Chest width (underarm to underarm): 11.5–12 inches across (roughly 23–24 inches total circumference)
- Bottom bag width: 16–18 inches across — you want a bell or pear shape so there's room for the legs to move
- Neck opening: 4.5–5 inches wide, with a 2–2.5 inch front drop and a 0.75–1 inch back drop
- Armholes: 4–4.5 inches deep along the side curve (about 8.5–9 inches total circumference)
- Shoulder straps: 2–2.5 inches wide

To draft it: sketch a basic tank-top bodice using those chest, shoulder, and neck numbers, then taper out from the base of the armhole into a wide, rounded bell toward the hem. Cut one back piece and either one front piece or two front halves if you're doing a center-front snap opening.

**Machine setup for thick, stretchy fleece**

Layering high-pile fleece with microfleece is going to want to stretch, slide, and pile up in the seams, so:

- **Needle:** a ballpoint/jersey or stretch needle, 90/14 or 100/16. The rounded tip slides between the knit fibers instead of snagging, and the heavier size punches through the pile cleanly.
- **Stitch:** a narrow zigzag (0.5–1.0 mm width) or your machine's built-in stretch/lightning stitch, so the seam has give and won't pop under stress.
- **Stitch length:** bump it up to 3.0–3.5 mm. Shorter stitches jam too much thread into the thick fabric and leave you with wavy, bunched seams.
- **Tension:** drop your upper thread tension a notch, from a standard 4 down to around 3 or 2.5, so the thread doesn't tunnel into the pile or pucker it.

**Getting the double layer to feed without bunching**

- A walking foot is worth digging out if you have one — it feeds the top and bottom layers at the same rate so the top fleece doesn't creep or stretch ahead of the bottom.
- If your presser foot pressure is adjustable, ease it off a bit so it's not fighting the bulk of the high-pile layer.
- Pin heavily — Wonder Clips or long ball-head pins every 1–2 inches will save you a lot of grief.
- For the snaps: fleece stretches, and that means metal prongs can tear right through the knit over time. Back every snap location with a small square of medium-weight woven interfacing or scrap cotton fused to the wrong side before you set the fastener, so it has something stable to bite into.
- For raw edges: fleece won't fray, so you can just fold the armholes and neckline under and stitch with a wide zigzag or twin needle, or bind them in lightweight knit bias tape if you want less bulk.

What's actually going on: a fully feathered robin sitting quietly on the ground is a fledgling, not an abandoned baby. This is normal — they leave the nest before they can fly well and spend a few days hopping around on the ground while the parents keep feeding and watching over them from nearby.

So here's what to do instead:

1. **Put it back outside now**, right where you found it near the hydrangeas, or tuck it into a low branch or dense shrub close by so it's out of view from cats.
2. **Deal with the cat problem** by keeping your own pets in and just watching from a window for a while. Parents usually swoop back in within an hour or two once things quiet down.
3. **Only if something's actually wrong** — it's bleeding, clearly hurt, or no parent shows up after 3–4 hours — should you hold off on the "put it back" plan. In that case, don't try feeding it anything; keep it warm, dark, and quiet in the box and get in touch with a licensed wildlife rehabber near you (ahnow.org can help you find one in the US).

**Quick heads up before you wire anything: don't put this between the amp head's speaker output and the cab.**

Standard Alpha pots are only rated for around 0.25–0.5W. Your Dual Rectifier's speaker output is pushing way more current and voltage than that into a 4–16Ω load. A 100kΩ pot sitting on the speaker line will fry almost instantly, and worse, it creates an open load condition that can take out your amp's output transformer. Real speaker-level attenuation needs a high-wattage reactive or resistive load — think 50–100W wirewound resistors or a proper 8/16Ω power L-pad, not a guitar-pedal-style pot.

---

### What this box is actually good for: an FX Loop volume control

Stick your 100k pot in the **Effects Loop**, between the preamp and power amp, instead. That's a spot where a standard audio pot is perfectly happy.

#### Wiring it up:

Looking at the back of the pot with the lugs pointing up (1 - 2 - 3, left to right):

```
       [ 100k Audio Pot ]
          (Rear View)
         [1]   [2]   [3]
          |     |     |
          |     |     +-----> Jack IN Tip (From Amp FX Send)
          |     +-----------> Jack OUT Tip (To Amp FX Return)
          +-----------------> Ground / Both Jack Sleeves & Enclosure
```

1. **Lug 3 (input):** goes to the Tip of the `IN` jack, which connects to the amp's **FX Send**.
2. **Lug 2 (wiper/output):** goes to the Tip of the `OUT` jack, which connects to the amp's **FX Return**.
3. **Lug 1 (ground):** ties to the Sleeve of both jacks, and to the metal enclosure itself.
4. Run a common ground wire between both jack sleeves.

#### How you'd use it:
1. Amp's **FX Send** → **Box IN**.
2. **Box OUT** → Amp's **FX Return**.
3. Cab stays plugged straight into the amp's speaker out, same as always.
4. Crank the Channel Master on the Dual Rectifier for that preamp saturation, and use this box in the loop to bring the overall volume down to something your neighbors can live with.

Running these dry on a stock high-speed (3450 RPM) bench grinder with vitrified wheels is going to cause you a few headaches: the tiger's eye (microcrystalline quartz) can thermally shock and crack, the grey aluminum oxide vitrified wheel will glaze over fast, and grinding chrysotile dry throws fine friable fibers into the air.

Lapidary stone really wants to be worked wet and slower than that — think 1725–1800 RPM — with silicon carbide or diamond abrasive. If you're bridging the gap before your CabKing arrives, the cheap fix is a router speed controller to bring the grinder down to around 1750 RPM, plus a gravity drip setup: a plastic bottle with an aquarium valve mounted above the wheel dripping onto the stone, and a tub underneath to catch runoff.

**Grit Progression**

**1. Rough shaping — 80–100 grit SiC**
Green SiC wheel, continuous drip. Knock off the outer rind and rough in your dome or profile, working in steady figure-eights so you don't groove the wheel face. 5–15 minutes a piece depending on how dense the material is and how much you're removing.

**2. Fine shaping / scratch removal — 220 grit SiC**
Wet 220 wheel. Smooth out the flat spots the 80 grit left. Towel the stone dry and check it under a strong single light to make sure every 80-grit scratch is gone before moving on. 5–10 minutes.

**3. Pre-polish / smoothing — 400 to 600 grit**
Flexible SiC belts or expandable rubber drums, wet — a hard vitrified wheel at this stage tends to leave flat spots that won't buff out.
- 400 grit clears the 220 scratches; you're aiming for an even matte surface. 3–5 minutes.
- 600 grit brings up a slight semi-gloss. Every trace of the earlier scratch pattern needs to be gone. 3–5 minutes.

**4. Pre-polish — 1200 grit**
Leather, felt, or a 1200-grit wet belt. This takes it from dull sheen to a smooth, low-luster surface that's ready for oxide. 2–3 minutes.

**Polishing and Compounds**

Run the hard felt buff damp — not dripping, not bone dry — and keep the RPM down, since tiger's eye can craze or crack under heat and chrysotile can scorch.

- **Tiger's eye (quartz-based):** Cerium oxide or high-purity aluminum oxide (Linde A). Mix a slurry about the consistency of thin milk, brush it onto the felt, and buff with moderate, steady pressure, keeping the stone moving so you don't burn the polish into one spot.
- **Chrysotile / serpentine (Mohs 2.5–4, soft):** Aluminum oxide works well here, tin oxide too. Use light pressure — this material is soft and fibrous, and heavy pressure or a dry buff will undercut along the banding.

Let's crunch the numbers on your fruit wash.

**What you're working with:**
* 4 bushels of stone fruit works out to roughly **180–200 lbs**.
* Peaches and apricots run a natural Brix that typically ferments out to about **5–6% ABV** with no added sugar.
* To land 1 gallon of finished 80–100 proof spirit off a pot still (once you make proper heads/tails cuts), you generally need **10–12 gallons of fruit wash**, which comes from roughly **80–100 lbs of crushed fruit**.

**So bottom line:** your 180–200 lbs is plenty. You're looking at something like **1.5 to 2 gallons** of finished, proofed brandy without adding a grain of sugar. Sugar only makes sense if you're trying to stretch your volume further or push the wash up to 8–10% ABV (what folks call a "sugar shine" or chaptalized wash) — just know that too much added sugar starts washing out the actual fruit character you're going for.

**A few things worth knowing before you mash everything up:**

1. **Mind the pits.** Don't let that drill mixer crack the stones open. Crushed pits leak amygdalin, which turns into cyanide compounds and harsh, bitter off-flavors during fermentation. Either pull the pits before mashing or run the mixer gently enough to strip flesh without splitting them open.

2. **Pectic enzyme is your friend.** Stone fruit is loaded with pectin. A dose of pectic enzyme before fermentation breaks down the pulp, frees up more juice, and bumps your liquid yield.

3. **Plan your still runs.** With 10–20 gallons of wash and only a 3-gallon boiler, you're looking at multiple stripping runs before you combine the low wines into one final spirit run. Strain out as much pulp as you can before you distill — otherwise you risk scorching the bottom of the pot.

Good instinct to double-check this before the drywall goes up. There's one thing you need to confirm first: **that the metal boxes are actually tied back to ground.**

A lot of 1954-era houses have metal boxes fed by old two-wire cable with no bare ground conductor, as opposed to grounded conduit or armored cable. If the box itself isn't connected to ground at the panel, screwing a pigtail into it just gives you the illusion of a ground — not an actual one.

**Quick test (30 seconds):**

Grab a multimeter or a basic voltage tester:
1. Restore power to the circuit.
2. Touch one lead to the hot wire (usually black) and the other to bare metal on the box — scratch off paint or grime if needed to get a clean contact point.
3. Read the result:
   - **~120V:** The box is grounded, probably through metallic conduit or armored cable. Your plan — pigtail into the threaded hole in the back of the box, other end to the green screw on the receptacle — is exactly right. Go ahead with all six.
   - **0V:** The box isn't grounded. A pigtail here just creates a floating ground, which won't actually protect your TV or receiver.

**If the box turns out ungrounded, here are your options:**

- **GFCI receptacle (fastest, code-compliant):** The NEC allows you to swap 2-prong outlets for 3-prong ones on an ungrounded circuit as long as the first outlet in the run is a GFCI (or the circuit's protected by a GFCI breaker). Wire it hot/neutral only, and stick the "No Equipment Ground" labels — they come in the box — on the covers. Keep in mind: GFCI protects you from shock, but it doesn't give your surge protector an actual path to ground for absorbing spikes.

- **Run new cable (best option for good AV gear):** Since the walls are open, this is the moment to pull new NM-B 14/2 or 12/2 with ground straight from the panel to these outlets. That gets your OLED and receiver a real equipment ground — better protection, less noise.

Run that test on the first box and you'll know exactly what you're dealing with — then you can knock out the rest of the room with confidence.

Great weekend project — 1920s craftsman sashes are worth saving. Just know that sanding through six layers of old paint indoors is going to load up your discs fast and throw a lot of fine dust into the living room, so plan for that.

**Sander picks (under $120, Home Depot, good dust ports):**

1. **Ridgid 5 in. Corded Random Orbital Sander (Model #R26011)** – ~$79. Heavy-duty motor, variable speed, active dust collection. Removes material quickly without beating up your wrists.
2. **DeWalt 5 in. Single Speed Random Orbital Sander (Model #DWE6421K)** – ~$89. 3-amp motor at 12,000 OPM, rubber overmold grip, sealed dust bag (or hook up a shop vac via the 1-1/4" adapter).

**Grit sequence:**
Start at **60 grit**, not 40 — 40 will gouge old-growth wood and leave swirls that are a pain to sand out later.

* **60 grit** – knocks down the bulk of the paint buildup
* **80–100 grit** – clears remaining residue, evens out the surface
* **150 grit** – preps bare wood for primer/paint or stain
* **220 grit (optional)** – final smoothing if you're staining/varnishing instead of painting

**Discs:** Regular sandpaper will clog almost immediately on old paint. Grab **Diablo 5 in. SandNet Discs** or **Diablo Ceramic Blend Discs** — both come in multi-packs at Home Depot. The SandNet ones can be rinsed or tapped clean when they gum up, so they last way longer on a heavy strip job like this.

**For the parts the round sander can't reach:**
Sash muntins, corners, and glazing lines need backup since a 5" disc will chew into the glass or profile detail if you're not careful.

* **Bahco Carbide Paint Scraper** (or the Husky 2-1/2 in. version) — a pull scraper that strips thick flaking paint dry, no dust, before the sander even comes out
* **Detail/contour sanding sponges (80 & 120 grit)** — perfect for tight inner corners and narrow muntins
* **Shop-Vac hookup** — since you're working inside, connect a wet/dry vac to the sander's dust port (HEPA filter if you have one) to keep the mess contained

That combo should get you through the stack of paint fast without wrecking the original wood detail underneath.

Quick flag before you grab the sandpaper: check your maintenance manual and Sensenich's service instructions first. Even small prop work can create stress concentrations if it's not done right, and depending on whether your aircraft is S-LSA or E-LSA, prop repairs generally need an A&P sign-off.

That said, assuming the pit really is minor — just barely catching a fingernail — and within allowable limits, here's the standard approach for dressing out leading-edge nicks on aluminum props, per FAA AC 43.13-1B and Sensenich's guidance:

**Tools:** Skip the aggressive file unless there's raised metal or an actual gouge. For something this shallow, a fine smooth-cut file (riffle or needle file) or a medium 240–320 grit abrasive cloth is usually enough to start. 400-grit alone will be too slow to get to the bottom of the pit — go 320, then 400, then finish with 600 for polishing.

**Blending:** You can't just sand the local spot. You need a smooth, gradual taper along the leading edge — roughly 10:1 to 20:1 length-to-depth — so you don't leave a flat spot or a new stress riser. Rough out the material to blend the damage into the surrounding contour, then do your final polishing strokes parallel to the blade length. This part matters: scratches running chordwise (across the blade) act like little stress risers and can seed fatigue cracks, so keep everything longitudinal on the finish pass.

**After you're done:** Inspect the area with a 10x loupe (or dye penetrant if you have it) to make sure the bottom of the pit is fully gone and there's no hairline cracking left behind. Bare aluminum needs to be protected right away too — Alodine or similar conversion coating, then touch-up prop paint, so it doesn't start pitting from corrosion.

Given that this is a stress-critical spot and you've got your first long solo XC Saturday, I'd have an A&P take a quick look tomorrow morning — nicks on the leading edge are focal points, and getting an experienced set of eyes on it means it's confirmed within tolerance and properly documented, so you're not carrying any doubt into the flight.

Hold off on the hydrated lime — please don't dump that in tonight.

Hydrated lime (calcium hydroxide) will spike your pH to somewhere north of 10-11, and that's a death sentence for the catfish the moment they hit the water Thursday. So before anything else: skip that plan entirely.

A couple of things worth knowing:

**Your fish will actually be fine in muddy water.** Channel catfish evolved in silty river systems — turbidity itself doesn't hurt their gills or suffocate them. What matters is dissolved oxygen, not clarity. So if you're worried about the fingerlings choking on clay, you can let that worry go. Stock them Thursday as planned; the chocolate-milk look isn't the threat you think it is.

**If you still want to clear the water, gypsum is the safe route.** Agricultural gypsum (calcium sulfate) flocculates clay without wrecking your pH the way lime does.

Math on your pond: 0.5 acres × 6 ft average depth = 3 acre-feet.

Typical gypsum rate runs 250–500 lbs per acre-foot depending on water hardness, so you're looking at roughly 750–1,500 lbs total — 15 to 30 of your 50-lb bags.

To apply it right: slurry it in water first and spread it across the surface rather than dumping dry bags in a pile. Expect it to take 3–7 days to fully settle the clay, so this won't get you clear water by Wednesday — just clear-ish water eventually.

**Alum is the fast option, but it's a tricky one.** Aluminum sulfate can drop clay out in 24–48 hours at around 50 lbs/acre-foot, which would actually hit your timeline. The catch is it swings pH acidic, hard enough that it normally needs to be buffered with hydrated lime in a strict 2:1 alum-to-lime ratio to keep the water from turning into a different kind of fish kill. With only 48 hours before your delivery, trying to dial in that buffer for the first time isn't something I'd recommend attempting.

**So here's what I'd actually do:** let the hatchery truck show up Thursday and stock into the murky water — it won't hurt them. Give the fingerlings a week or two to settle in, then treat the pond with gypsum at your own pace to clear it up safely, without the pH gymnastics.

Removing metal from the locking lugs changes headspace, and on a magnum cartridge like .300 Win Mag that pushes pretty serious pressure, an excessive-headspace condition isn't something to risk right before an elk hunt. Since the rifle cycled fine last season, a factory tolerance issue or burr showing up out of nowhere isn't the likely culprit anyway. Let's figure out what's actually going on before touching the action.

**First, close the bolt on an empty chamber.**
- Smooth? Then it's something about the ammo, the chamber itself, or how the extractor/ejector is engaging the case head.
- Still binds? Look at:
  - **Scope base screws** — if you mounted or torqued a base recently, the front screw might be poking into the receiver ring and fouling the lug raceway.
  - **Front action screw** — make sure it hasn't backed out or been driven in too far near the lug area.
  - **Bolt shroud/firing pin** — pull the bolt apart, clean out any old hardened grease, and re-lube lightly with a good synthetic oil.

**Second, check the bolt face and ejector.** The T3x uses a spring-loaded plunger ejector and a sliding-plate extractor. Look for brass shavings or carbon built up under the extractor hook or around the ejector plunger — a sticky plunger will fight compression right as the bolt cams down, which lines up with that last-quarter-inch bind you're describing. While you're in there, a small dab of a high-pressure gun grease (TW25B, Lucas Gun Grease) on the rear lug surfaces helps too — dry lugs under load can bind more than people expect.

**Third, think about a carbon ring in the chamber.** Belted magnums are notorious for building up a hard ring right at the case-mouth junction or the throat, even when the rest of the chamber looks spotless. If a round's pressing into that ring, you'll get resistance closing the bolt — and a pressure spike when it fires. Scrub the throat with a real carbon solvent (Bore Tech C4, Slip 2000 Carbon Killer) and an oversized bronze or nylon chamber brush.

**Fourth, look hard at the ammo itself.** .300 Win Mag headspaces off the belt, so small variations in factory brass, oxidation on ammo that's a year old, or seating depth differences can all cause a hard chamber. Try a fresh box of the same load and see if it still binds. Also check the rounds you've already cycled under good light — shiny rub marks on the belt, shoulder, neck, or bullet ogive will tell you exactly where the contact is happening.

If you go through all of that — screws checked, bolt face and ejector cleaned, lugs lightly greased — and it's still binding on empty or across different ammo, get it to a gunsmith to check headspace with Go/No-Go gauges before you zero it.

Hold on — before we get to knots, I'd really push back on the "crank it dead straight with a winch" plan. Pulling an 80ft wire span guitar-string tight between a chimney and a live tree is asking for trouble, and here's the physics of why:

1. **Catenary math is brutal.** Getting an 80ft span down to near-zero sag takes tension in the hundreds to thousands of pounds. Something's going to give — your Dacron, the antenna wire, or the chimney mount itself.
2. **The oak moves more than you think.** A big limb can sway 2–4 feet in a decent wind. If there's zero slack in the system, the tree becomes a lever arm that can rip your chimney bricks loose or pop the wire instantly.

So instead of anchoring it rigid, here's how I'd actually rig it:

**Put a pulley (or halyard) up in the tree.** A small UV-rated pulley, or even just a smooth ring, with the Dacron run through it, so the line can move instead of locking solid.

**Give it something to pull against.** Either hang a counterweight on the ground/tree side — a 5–10 lb sash weight, lead weight, jug of concrete, whatever — a few feet off the ground, or splice in a heavy antenna spring or mooring snubber. As the oak sways, the weight or spring travels up and down and keeps tension roughly constant without ever overloading the chimney.

**Let it sag a little.** 2–3% of the span — call it 1.5 to 2.5 feet of droop over 80ft — is genuinely fine and takes a ton of stress off both ends.

Now, to your actual question — the knot:

- **Bowline**: still my pick. Forms a solid non-slip loop and comes untied even after serious loading.
- **Round turn and two half hitches**: good if you're wrapping directly around the limb — the round turn eats the friction/load so the hitches stay easy to undo later.
- **Buntline hitch**: compact, won't shake loose in wind, but can jam tighter than a bowline under heavy load.

Bottom line: bowline for the knot, pulley in the tree, skip the winch, and let a counterweight or spring do the tensioning instead — your chimney will thank you.

Hold off — don't put any isopropyl alcohol on those 78s, even diluted.

Your regular 33s are PVC vinyl, so alcohol's fine on them. But 78s from the 1930s are made of **shellac**, and alcohol is essentially a solvent for shellac. Even a light 20% mix will start softening and eating away at the grooves — you'd be looking at permanent, gray, mushy damage, not just a bad clean.

Here's what to use instead:

### Safe Cleaning Method
1. **Mix up a gentler solution:**
   * Warm distilled water with just 1–2 drops of a mild, unscented, dye-free dish soap (plain Dawn works) per quart.
   * Or go with a non-ionic surfactant made for archival use, like Tergitol 15-S-9, or a dedicated alcohol-free record cleaner.
2. **Work the grooves:**
   * Dip a soft-bristled brush — goat hair or a soft paintbrush — into the soapy water.
   * Clean in gentle circles, following the direction of the grooves.
   * Avoid the paper label — water can dissolve old glue and wreck it.
3. **Rinse:**
   * Go over the record with a microfiber cloth dampened in plain distilled water (no soap) to lift off residue.
4. **Dry:**
   * Pat dry with a clean, dry microfiber cloth, or stand them in a dish rack on a towel to air dry fully before you sleeve or play them.

Great haul, by the way — jazz and blues 78s from that era are a real find. Just skip the alcohol and you'll keep them in playable shape.

Before we get to the math — **don't do this in standard 12oz pry-off bottles.** Those bottles top out around 2.5–3.0 volumes of CO2. At 4.5 volumes you'd be looking at 50+ PSI at room temp, and that's bottle bomb territory — genuinely dangerous, not just "might gush a little."

If you want to actually hit 4.5 volumes, you'd need real pressure-rated vessels: heavy Champagne bottles with wire cages, or a keg. That's the only safe route to the number you asked for.

**The math itself**, for reference:

1. Residual CO2 in the beer at 68°F: ~0.86 volumes
2. CO2 you still need to add: 4.5 − 0.86 = 3.64 volumes
3. Formula: grams of dextrose = gallons × (target − residual) × 15.19

So: 5 × 3.64 × 15.19 ≈ **276 g (9.7 oz)** — but again, only pour that into bottles rated to hold it.

**For your actual 12oz pry-offs**, here's what's safe:

- Russian Imperial Stout style range is typically 1.8–2.4 volumes. For 2.2 volumes, use about **102 g (3.6 oz)** of corn sugar.
- The ceiling for standard bottles is roughly 2.7 volumes, which would take about **140 g (4.9 oz)**.

However much you use, dissolve it in 1–2 cups of boiling water, let it cool a bit, then rack the beer onto it gently in the bottling bucket. And double-check fermentation is fully finished before you bottle.

Lowe's and Home Depot both stock these in the drainage/plumbing aisle, usually labeled something like "2 in. x 3 in. to 4 in. Corrugated Downspout Adapter."

A few things worth keeping in mind while you're doing this:

1. **Check with your neighbor first.** French drains are generally meant for slow groundwater drainage, not the sudden gush of a roof downspout during a heavy storm. Piping your runoff straight into theirs could overload it and send water backing up somewhere neither of you wants it.
2. **Go with solid pipe, not perforated, for the bridge.** You want the water to actually travel the 8 feet to the drain instead of leaking out into the ground right next to your walkway.
3. **Don't skip the slope.** Aim for at least a 1/4 inch drop per foot — around 2 inches total over your run — so water and debris keep moving instead of sitting in the pipe.

Skip the iron entirely — please don't put heat on this stuff.

Those "Eastman Nitrate" edge markings mean you're holding cellulose nitrate film, which is genuinely flammable and heat-reactive. Ironing it, even through fabric or parchment, risks melting the base, warping the emulsion, or worse.

There are two better routes, both using stuff you already have lying around.

**Weight it down with glass right on the scanner**

This is the quickest fix if you just want the curl gone long enough to scan:

1. Grab a small pane of glass from a cheap photo frame (4x6 or 5x7 works fine). Wipe off any sharp edges, clean it well, and let it dry.
2. Lay the negative on the scanner bed emulsion-side down — dull side down, shiny side up.
3. Set the glass on top. Its weight is enough to press the strip flat against the glass without you having to touch or stress the film.
4. Close the lid (or if it won't sit flush, drape a dark cloth over the gap) and scan as normal.

**Or flatten them first under books, over a few days**

If you'd rather de-curl the whole batch before you start scanning:

1. Slide each negative into a paper envelope, or sandwich it between sheets of smooth, acid-free printer paper — don't let negatives touch each other.
2. Set the paper sandwiches on a flat, hard surface somewhere cool and ventilated, and stack heavy books on top — encyclopedias, hardcovers, whatever's dense.
3. Give it 48 to 72 hours. Plain pressure at room temperature will relax the curl without any heat involved.

**A couple of nitrate-specific notes:**
- Keep them somewhere cool and airy, away from sunlight, heaters, or anything with a flame.
- Handle by the edges only — skin oils on the emulsion aren't good for it.

Hold up — don't put bar and chain oil in that gas mix.

Bar oil is a thick, tacky lubricant made to cling to a chainsaw's guide bar. It's not formulated to combust or mix properly with gasoline. Run it through a 2-stroke and you'll foul the plug, gunk up the carb, and likely kill the engine on your brand new blower pretty fast.

What you actually need is real 2-cycle engine oil — Echo PowerBlend, Stihl 2-Cycle, anything rated JASO-FD or ISO-L-EGD works fine.

As for the math, once you've got the right oil:

- Ratio: 50:1
- Gas: 2 gallons (256 fl oz)
- Oil needed: 5.12 fl oz (basically 5.1–5.2 oz)

Most 2-cycle oil bottles are sold in that exact 5.2 oz size so you don't even have to measure — one bottle per 2 gallons and you're set.

Two problems with that batch as loaded:

1. **Quartz + glass is a bad mix.** Quartz sits around Mohs 7, sea glass is more like 5.5, so the quartz will just chip and grind the glass down instead of tumbling nicely alongside it. Glass really wants to run with ceramic media or by itself, not rock.

2. **7 days of coarse in Stage 1 is way too aggressive for glass.** That 60/90 grit stage is built for hard rock — a week of it will basically sand your sea glass into nothing. Glass schedules normally skip that stage entirely, or only spend a day or two in it at most.

Given both of those, this isn't a "tweak the timing and go" situation right now — I wouldn't run it as-is.

Let's run the numbers on sealant, batteries, and a couple of things worth flagging before you finalize this build.

**Sealant volume (700x55 on 23mm internal rims)**

Target 90–100 ml per tire, and don't go below 75–80 ml.

Here's the reasoning: a 55mm tire has a lot more internal surface area than the 40mm gravel tires most sealant guidance assumes, so anything under ~75 ml won't hold enough of a liquid pool to coat the casing and hit a puncture instantly as the wheel spins. On top of that, the Rene Herse Extralight casing is thin enough that it weeps and soaks up a meaningful chunk of your initial fill during the first few days. And at 4,000m+, the dry air and low pressure speed up evaporation — Orange Seal Endurance holds up better than most formulas, but under 90 ml you're risking it drying to a skin within 3–4 weeks, which is well inside your resupply gaps.

**Tires and spares — a reality check**

Don't skip emergency tire repairs. No amount of sealant will close a sidewall slice or a flint pinch flat over 3–4mm, and being stuck above 4,000m without a backup plan for that is genuinely dangerous.

The lightweight fix: carry two TPU tubes (Tubolito S-Tubo or Schwalbe Aerothan, ~45g each) plus a small Dynaplug tool and a few adhesive boots/patches. That's under 120g total — cheap insurance for how remote this route is.

Also worth reconsidering: Extralight casings are wonderfully supple, but Peru's shale and rocky doubletrack are known for slicing sidewalls. If you haven't placed the order yet, Endurance or Endurance Plus casing might be the smarter call — the extra 60–80g per tire is a fair trade against a structural failure out there.

**AXS battery strategy**

One mounted + one spare (two total) plus a compact USB charging cradle is the right call. A third battery is unnecessary weight.

Rough runtime: an AXS rear derailleur battery is good for about 60 hours of riding, roughly 1,000–1,500km of shifting. Cold nights in the Andes will drain lithium-ion capacity faster than you'd expect, so pull the mounted battery (and keep the spare) somewhere warm overnight — inside your sleeping bag or a pocket close to your body works.

Don't forget a spare CR2032 for the shifters too — they're about 3g, no reason to leave it behind.

**One more thing: your gearing**

A 10-44t XPLR cassette paired with a standard 38–40t 1x chainring gives you a lowest gear around 0.86–0.90. On sustained unpaved climbs above 10–15% grade at 4,500m+, loaded down, that's going to feel brutal. If there's still time before you order, an AXS Mullet setup — Eagle AXS rear derailleur with a 10-52t cassette — gets you down to a much friendlier 0.73 low gear for this kind of terrain.

Love that your son's into this stuff, but I have to stop you before you order that microscope: **there's no light microscope on Earth, at any price, that will let you see a bacteriophage.**

Here's the physics behind that, plus a better plan for his birthday.

### Why light just can't do it
Bacteriophages are viruses, and they're absurdly small — usually **20 to 200 nanometers** across. Light itself has a hard resolution ceiling here, called the Abbe diffraction limit, sitting around **200 nanometers**. Below that, you're not looking at a blurry version of the object anymore — you're looking at nothing, because the wavelength of visible light literally can't resolve it. To actually see that famous "spider" or "lunar lander" shape of a phage docking onto a cell, you need an **electron microscope (TEM or Cryo-EM)** — the kind of equipment that runs tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars, not $48.

### About that "2500X"
That number is what's called **empty magnification** — magnifying a fuzzy image bigger doesn't make it sharper, it just makes the blur bigger too. Real optical microscopes, even good ones with oil immersion and quality glass, top out at a *useful* magnification around **1000X–1250X**. Anything claiming 2000X–2500X, especially with acrylic or resin lenses instead of glass, is just going to hand you a dim, distorted, useless smear of an image.

### What he can actually do
He won't get to watch phages swimming around in real time, but there's a genuine, classic experiment that's very much within reach: the **plaque assay**.
* Grow a lawn of safe host bacteria (something like non-pathogenic *E. coli*) across a petri dish.
* Add a sample containing phages — they'll infect and burst the bacteria in their immediate area, leaving behind clear little circles called **plaques**. That's your visible, countable proof of phage activity.
* If you still want to get him a microscope he can actually use — for looking at protozoa, amoebas, rotifers, or basic bacterial morphology — skip the AliExpress special and look at an entry-level compound scope with **real glass optics, an Abbe condenser, and an adjustable mechanical stage**. Brands like AmScope, Swift, or OMAX in the **$100–$150** range are solid, reliable starting points.

Either a plaque assay kit or a proper glass-optic starter scope would make a genuinely great birthday gift and fit right into what he's already interested in.

So, bad news: that math doesn't actually get you through the night. Two (or even three) 100Ah lead-acid marine batteries will run that heater for something like 30-45 minutes, not 8 hours.

Here's where it falls apart:

**The real energy budget:** 1500W at 12V is closer to 125-140A once you account for inverter losses. Run that for 8 hours and you're looking at roughly 1,000Ah of *usable* 12V power needed. That's the number that matters, not just the instantaneous draw.

**Why lead-acid can't deliver it:**
- Deep-cycle marine batteries only give you about 50% of rated capacity before you start damaging them. So two 100Ah batteries = 100Ah usable, not 200Ah.
- On top of that, yanking 125+ amps out of a small lead-acid bank causes serious voltage sag (Peukert's Law in action), and that'll trip your inverter's low-voltage shutoff well before you run out of actual battery.

**What I'd do instead for winter van life:**
- **Diesel/gas parking heater** (Chinese diesel heater, Webasto, Espar) — this is the standard answer for a reason. Taps your fuel tank, sips fuel, and only pulls 1-3A on the DC side to run the fan. Your two 100Ah batteries would handle that for multiple nights, easily.
- **12V heated mattress pad/blanket** — these only draw 40-60W (3-5A). Combine with a solid sub-zero bag and a 200Ah bank will carry you through the night with room to spare.
- **Mr. Heater Buddy (propane)** — decent stopgap, but you need to crack a window for ventilation and have a CO detector running.

Bottom line for sub-freezing Rockies nights: ditch the ceramic space heater plan and go with a vented fuel heater or heated bedding instead. The numbers just don't work for a resistance heater off a small battery bank.

Before we get into the noise reduction numbers, two things need to be flagged first — and then I'll give you a better restoration workflow than what you've got.

**First: please don't throw out the shellac.** If these are the only surviving copies of local radio performances, those discs are primary historical artifacts, not just a source file. Archivally, a digitized copy never really substitutes for a unique physical original — future transfer equipment (optical scanning, specialized styli) will be able to pull more off the groove than anything you're getting today, and the digitization itself only ever captures one interpretation of the groove, not the artifact. If storage is the real constraint, look at deaccessioning to a university library, state historical society, or an ARSC-member sound archive — even the Library of Congress. Institutions like that are generally glad to take unique historical recordings rather than see them scrapped.

**Second: your hardware is working against you.** The AT-LP60XUSB has two issues for 78s from this era:

1. **Stylus size** — the stock cartridge on the LP60X is a 0.6 mil microgroove stylus, built for modern vinyl. 78s need roughly a 3.0 mil stylus. With the wrong size, the needle rides in the dirty, worn floor of the groove instead of tracking the sidewalls — that's a big part of your "frying bacon" sound, and it can also grind more wear into the shellac.
2. **Speed and EQ** — the LP60X doesn't play at 78 RPM natively, so if you sped it up after recording at 45, that's fine mechanically, but the turntable's preamp is applying a modern RIAA curve, not the varied proprietary curves 1930s shellac actually used.

**Now, onto the noise reduction itself.** Chasing "Spotify clean" silence on a 1930s shellac transfer is going to introduce its own problems — underwater/bubbling artifacts, chewed-up transients, hollow-sounding vocals. A Low Pass Filter anywhere from 2.5–3.5 kHz at a 24 dB slope will strip out presence, sibilance, and the upper harmonics of the voices and instruments along with the hiss. And pushing a noise gate hard enough to get true silence between tracks will introduce audible pumping and breathing as it snaps open and shut.

Here's the chain I'd use instead:

**Step 1 — De-click before anything else.**
Don't run Noise Reduction first; big clicks throw off the noise profile the algorithm builds. Go to *Effect > Volume and Compression > Click Removal*, start around Threshold 200, Max Spike Width 20, and adjust until the pops are tamed without dulling brass or percussion transients.

**Step 2 — Gentler spectral noise reduction.**
Grab a clean noise sample from a stretch of pure groove noise before the music starts (*Effect > Noise Removal and Repair > Noise Reduction > Get Noise Profile*), then apply it to the whole track with more conservative settings than what you've been running:
- Reduction: 6–12 dB (18 dB is pushing you into phase artifacts)
- Sensitivity: 6.00
- Frequency smoothing: 3–6 bands

It's better to leave a faint, even bed of groove noise underneath than to push hard enough to create digital distortion.

**Step 3 — EQ instead of a hard low-pass.**
Skip the steep low-pass at 3.5 kHz. 1930s electrical recordings usually carry useful signal up to somewhere around 6–7.5 kHz. Use *Effect > EQ and Filters > Filter Curve EQ* and apply a gentle high-shelf starting around 6 kHz, dropping -6 to -12 dB, to tame hiss without gutting vocal clarity. Add a High Pass Filter at 50 Hz (12 dB/octave) to clear out turntable rumble on the low end.

**Step 4 — Silence between tracks.**
Forget the gate for this. Manually fade each track in (0.5–1s) and out (1–2s), and if you need clean gaps between files, just export the tracks separately rather than trying to force silence with a gate mid-playback.

Stop right there — don't wire it that way. What that forum guy described is a "bootleg ground," and it's genuinely dangerous, not just technically against code.

Here's the problem with it: that jumper wire just ties your ground pin to neutral. Under normal conditions it might even test as "grounded" on a cheap plug-in tester. But if the neutral ever loosens or fails anywhere upstream in that circuit, the return current has nowhere to go except through the ground pin — which means the metal case of your PC, monitor, or anything else plugged in could suddenly become energized at full 120V. Anyone touching it gets shocked. On top of that, your surge protector needs an actual path to earth to do its job; a bootleg ground doesn't give it one, so instead of protecting your gear from a surge, you could end up with damaged equipment or a fire risk.

So here's what's actually safe to do instead:

**Option 1 — GFCI outlet (the practical fix for most people in your situation):**
Put in a GFCI receptacle where the old 2-prong one was, even with no ground wire present. Black goes to LINE hot (brass screw), white to LINE neutral (silver screw), and just leave the green ground screw empty. There should be stickers in the GFCI box — use the one that says "No Equipment Ground" and slap it on the cover plate. This will absolutely protect you from a dangerous shock. The tradeoff is that since there's still no real earth ground behind it, you won't get full surge suppression for sensitive electronics like a nice PC.

**Option 2 — just replace it with another 2-prong outlet:**
If the old one was simply worn out, hardware stores still sell ungrounded 2-prong receptacles. Keeps things simple and code-compliant for what you've got.

**Option 3 — run an actual grounded circuit (the real fix if you want true surge protection):**
For genuine equipment grounding and surge protection on something like a gaming or work PC, you'd want an electrician to run new Romex with a bare ground wire back to the panel. And honestly, since you're still on the original 1948 fuse box, it wouldn't hurt to have an electrician take a look at that too while they're at it — that's a separate conversation, but worth having.

Quick but important stop first: **don't mix bleach and vinegar.** That combo produces chlorine gas almost instantly, and it's genuinely dangerous to breathe — burns to the lungs, respiratory distress, the works — especially somewhere small and enclosed like a shut laundry closet. So that recipe's off the table entirely.

Here's what I'd actually do instead:

**Option 1: Washing soda + degreaser soak**
Grease wants an alkaline degreaser, and mildew wants hot water plus oxygen cleaners, so:
1. Fill the tub with very hot water, add about 1/2 cup washing soda (baking soda works in a pinch) plus a heavy-duty detergent or a few tablespoons of Dawn dish soap.
2. Let the towels sit for several hours or overnight — this is gentle on cotton, no fiber damage from long soak times like you'd get with bleach.
3. Follow up with a normal hot-water wash cycle.

**Option 2: Vinegar and bleach, but never together — two separate cycles**
If you want both the odor-killing power of vinegar and the sanitizing/whitening of bleach, run them back to back, never combined:
1. First cycle: hot water wash with 1 cup white vinegar, no detergent, to strip buildup and kill mildew smell.
2. Second cycle: normal detergent plus 1/3 to 1/2 cup regular bleach in the dispenser (or diluted in water) to sanitize and whiten.

One more thing on cotton and bleach specifically: don't soak it in a strong bleach solution for 10-12 hours regardless of what you mix it with. Extended bleach exposure breaks down cellulose fibers over time — you'll end up with weak spots, fraying, even holes. Keep any bleach contact limited to a normal 10-15 minute wash cycle, not an overnight soak.

Hold off on that mixture — don't spray it on your trees while they're in bloom.

Putting these three ingredients together right now would hurt your pollinators, damage the trees themselves, and still wouldn't touch the codling moth problem. Let me explain why, then walk through what actually works.

**Why this plan backfires:**

1. **Sulfur + oil = burned trees.** Sulfur and horticultural oils like neem should never be combined, and ideally shouldn't even be applied within 14–30 days of each other. Mixed together, they cause serious chemical burn on leaves, blossoms, and any fruit that's trying to form.

2. **You'd be killing the pollinators you need.** Spraying oil or soap directly onto open flowers suffocates bees and other pollinators on contact. Without them, your Honeycrisp blossoms won't set fruit — so you'd be trading a worm problem for a no-apples problem.

3. **Wrong pest, wrong timing.** Codling moths don't do their damage during bloom. Adults emerge and lay eggs on leaves and young fruitlets after the petals drop — so spraying open flowers does nothing to stop them.

**What to do instead, organically:**

Wait until petal fall — once 75–100% of the blossoms have dropped — before you start treating.

*Timing window:* Adult moths generally emerge around petal fall, and eggs hatch about 10–14 days after that (or roughly 250 degree-days from the first sustained catch in a pheromone trap). That's the window when larvae are trying to bore into the fruit.

*Products that actually work post-bloom:*
- **Spinosad** (Captain Jack's Deadbug Brew is a common brand) — the strongest organic option against codling moth larvae. Start at petal fall, reapply every 7–10 days per the label, and spray at dusk so you're not hitting foraging bees.
- **Codling Moth Granulovirus** (Cyd-X) — a biological control that only affects codling moth larvae specifically. Completely safe for bees and other beneficials.
- **Neem oil on its own**, if you want to use what's already in your shed: mix 2 tablespoons neem oil with 1 teaspoon mild liquid soap (just as an emulsifier) per gallon of water. Spray at dawn or dusk when it's under 85°F to avoid leaf burn. And make sure no sulfur has touched the tree in the previous 30 days.

*Beyond spraying:*
- **Bag the fruit.** Once fruitlets are dime- or nickel-sized (thinning time), slip individual apple bags or nylon barrier socks over them. This gets you close to full protection with no spraying at all.
- **Clean up drops.** Pick up and destroy any fruit that falls throughout June and July — that breaks the moth's life cycle before it can complete another generation.

**Hold on — before you tape anything up, this setup shouldn't run as-is.** There's a serious overload and fire risk here, separate from the rain question entirely.

**The math doesn't work.** Commercial catering warmers usually pull 1,000–1,500 watts each — that's 8.5 to 12.5 amps apiece. Four of them plus the DJ's PA and mixer means you're asking for 4,000–6,000+ watts through this setup. Your 16-gauge, 100-foot cord, though, is only rated for about 10 amps — roughly 1,200 watts total. Long thin cords like that lose a lot of capacity over distance. You're not going to trip a breaker so much as overheat and potentially melt that cord well before you get there, and a standard garage circuit (15–20A) can't cover this load anyway.

What actually needs to change:
- **Split the load across circuits.** Ideally each warmer gets its own dedicated 15A/20A line — realistically, no more than one warmer per household circuit. That likely means running separate heavy-duty cords from different outlets, possibly different houses (garages, kitchens, laundry rooms).
- **Go up in gauge.** For a 100-foot run, you want 12-gauge or even 10-gauge cord, not 16.
- **Keep the DJ gear on its own circuit**, away from the warmers — mixing them invites both hum and trips.
- **If you can't get multiple dedicated lines**, switch the food warmers over to Sterno/chafing fuel instead of electric.

**On the rain question specifically:** skip the electrical tape and the grocery bag — neither is actually watertight, and a bag will just trap moisture inside and create a short/shock risk sitting there in wet grass. Better moves:
- Get the plug/strip connection up off the ground entirely — set it on a bucket, crate, or under a table inside the tent.
- If a connection absolutely has to stay outdoors, raise it on a brick and cover it with an upside-down plastic bin, notched at the edge for the cords to pass through.
- Confirm the source outlet is GFCI-protected — most exterior outlets are, but it's worth checking, since that's your real protection against shock in damp conditions, not tape.

Short answer: Windows doesn't expose a registry key or built-in PowerShell command for BD PROCHOT — it's an Intel MSR (`0x1FC`) enforced at the firmware/hardware level, so touching it means going through a ring-0 kernel driver, not a simple toggle.

That 0.79 GHz cliff you're seeing is textbook stuck-PROCHOT behavior — usually caused by a bad sensor reading, an underpowered/third-party charger, or DPTF being overly aggressive. Here's how to actually get out of it:

---

### Step 1: Kill Intel Dynamic Tuning / DPTF

DPTF will downclock the CPU on its own logic regardless of your Windows power plan, so it needs to go first.

1. Open PowerShell as Administrator.
2. Disable the relevant services:
   ```powershell
   Get-Service -Name "*DPTF*", "*DynamicTuning*" | Set-Service -StartupType Disabled -PassThru | Stop-Service
   ```
3. Open Device Manager (`devmgmt.msc`).
4. Under **System devices**, find:
   - `Intel(R) Dynamic Tuning Processor Participant`
   - `Intel(R) Dynamic Platform and Thermal Framework Processor Participant`
5. Right-click and **Disable** (don't uninstall — Windows will just put it back on reboot).

---

### Step 2: Clear BD PROCHOT with ThrottleStop

Since this bit lives at the MSR level, you need a tool that ships its own signed driver to reach it.

1. Grab **ThrottleStop** — it's portable, no install needed.
2. Launch `ThrottleStop.exe`.
3. Uncheck **BD PROCHOT** in the main panel.
4. Hit **Save**, then **Turn On**.
5. Clock speed should snap back up from 0.79 GHz to normal base/boost almost immediately.

*Heads up: TJMax thermal shutoff (~100°C) stays active no matter what — unchecking BD PROCHOT doesn't remove that hard stop, just the soft throttle.*

---

### Step 3: Force max performance at the OS level

Make sure Windows itself isn't adding another layer of throttling on top.

1. In an elevated PowerShell, unlock the hidden Ultimate Performance plan:
   ```powershell
   powercfg -duplicatescheme e9a42b02-d5df-448d-aa00-03f14749eb61
   ```
2. Select it from `powercfg.cpl`.
3. Go to **Change plan settings > Change advanced power settings**:
   - **Processor power management > System cooling policy** — set both AC and DC to **Active**.
   - **Minimum processor state** — set to `100%`.

---

### Worth checking on the hardware side too
- **Charger:** if you're on a USB-C dock or a non-Dell brick, swap to the real Dell power adapter plugged straight into the laptop. Underpowered charging is a common PROCHOT trigger.
- **Airflow:** prop the back of the laptop up an inch or two so the intake vents aren't smothered during the multi-hour run.

Hold off on the plate screws for a second — two things here need to change before you power this back up.

**Skip the sheet-metal-screw-to-box grounding idea.** A 1954 house with two-wire cloth wiring almost certainly has an ungrounded box, so running a pigtail to it wouldn't actually give you a real ground — you'd just be grounding the receptacle to nothing. On top of that, the NEC doesn't allow self-tapping or sheet metal screws as a grounding method anyway. The fix is simpler than what you were planning: leave the green screw empty. A GFCI protects you by watching for imbalance between hot and neutral, and it does that job fully even with zero ground wire connected.

**You do need the "No Equipment Ground" sticker — here's why it still matters.** Your instinct makes sense: if the GFCI is already keeping you safe from shock, why bother labeling anything? But the sticker isn't there to warn about shock risk — that's covered. It's there because the third prong on that outlet still doesn't connect to a real equipment ground path back to the panel, and some equipment (surge protectors being the classic example) relies on that ground to function as advertised, separate from the shock protection a GFCI gives you. NEC 406.4(D)(2) requires the sticker precisely because "GFCI-protected" and "grounded" are two different things, and anyone plugging something in later has no way to tell the difference just by looking at the outlet. So it goes on.

Here's the full sequence to finish the job:

1. **Confirm the power's actually off.** Breaker off, then check with your multimeter across the wires and from each wire to the box — zero volts before you touch anything.
2. **Neutral to line silver.** The white (or ribbed/identified) wire goes to the top silver LINE WHITE terminal.
3. **Hot to line brass.** Black wire to top brass LINE HOT.
4. **Leave the yellow tape alone.** No downstream devices, so LOAD stays capped off.
5. **Ground screw stays empty.** Nothing gets connected there.
6. **Seat it in the box.** Fold the old cloth-insulated wires back in gently — that insulation gets brittle with age — then screw the GFCI into the box.
7. **Plate and sticker.** Put the wall plate on, and stick the "No Equipment Ground" label onto the plate or receptacle.
8. **Power up and test.** Flip the breaker, hit RESET on the GFCI, then TEST to confirm it trips, then reset it and you're done.

For clearing 4 acres of cedar and brush, here's what I'd point you toward, plus how to actually use one of these things without setting yourself on fire.

### Torches Worth Buying Under $50
* **Harbor Freight Greenwood 500,000 BTU Propane Torch with Push Button Igniter (~$30–$35)** — this is basically the default choice for cheap brush torches, and for good reason. Flow valve, turbo trigger handle (squeeze it for full blast), and a 10-foot hose that hooks straight to a standard 20 lb tank.
* **Flame King or AUSAIL 500,000 BTU Torch with Turbo Trigger (~$35–$45, Amazon)** — basically the same formula: push-button ignition, 10-ft hose.

Whichever one you land on, make sure it has a **turbo/boost trigger** and a hose that's at least **6.5–10 feet**, so the tank can sit well away from heat and embers.

### How to Actually Burn These Piles

**Cedar is not a polite fuel.** It's loaded with resin and will pop violently and throw sparks once it catches. Don't stand over the pile or downwind when you light it.

**Cut a firebreak before anything else.** Rake or shovel a bare-dirt ring at least 10–15 feet around each pile — tractor bucket if you've got one. Also worth checking wind conditions before you start; you want it under 8–10 mph.

**Use the torch to ignite, not to burn.** Don't waste propane trying to torch whole logs or the outer branches. Get the nozzle down into the bottom interior of the pile, into the dry fine tinder and twigs, and hold the flame there for 30–60 seconds until you've got a solid coal bed going. After that, the draft does the work for you.

**Respect the tank.** Keep it upright the entire time — tip it over and you risk feeding liquid propane to the nozzle instead of vapor, which means an uncontrolled flare. Keep it at the far end of the hose, away from radiant heat and out of the wind's path toward the fire. Gloves, eye protection, and natural-fiber clothing only — no synthetics that'll melt onto you.

**Have water on hand before you strike anything.** A charged hose, a backpack sprayer, or a few 5-gallon buckets with a shovel nearby so you can knock down any embers that get away from you.
