Quick heads up before you check out at Home Depot: mounting the 49:1 unun box flush against that metal chimney is going to cause problems. The metal pipe will couple capacitively with the unun, detuning it, driving your SWR way up, and potentially feeding RF back into your house wiring or ductwork. You'll want a non-conductive standoff between the unun and the chimney rather than strapping it straight on.

Here's what to grab and how to put it together:

### Shopping List

1. **Chimney strapping:** stainless steel band clamps sized for your chimney's diameter, or a galvanized chimney strap kit.
2. **Standoff mast:** a 2–3 ft length of 1-1/4" Schedule 40 PVC pipe. This gets the unun a foot or two clear of the metal.
3. **Box-to-mast hardware:** UV-rated black cable ties or stainless hose clamps to fasten the unun box onto the PVC.
4. **Tree-end rigging (don't skip this):** a small rope-rated marine/utility pulley, 50–100 ft of braided polyester/Dacron rope (skip standard nylon or polypro — it breaks down fast in sunlight), and either a heavy-duty bungee or an eye bolt with a spring/counterweight setup. Oaks sway a lot, and a rigid line will eventually tear your wire or the unun connection apart.
5. **Weatherproofing:** self-fusing silicone tape (or Coax-Seal) plus a good outdoor electrical tape like Scotch Super 33+ for the SO-239/PL-259 joint.

### Putting It Up

1. **Chimney standoff:** Clamp the PVC pipe upright to the chimney using two hose clamps near the base, leaving the top 12–18 inches clear of the metal.
2. **Mount the unun:** Attach the unun box to the top of the PVC using clamps or heavy zip ties.
3. **Manage strain:** Don't let wire tension pull on the unun's terminal screw — anchor the wire eyelet there, but route the actual pulling force to a strain-relief point on the PVC mast itself.
4. **Tree end:** Get the pulley up high in the oak, thread your Dacron rope through it to the far-end insulator, and use the bungee or a counterweight at the ground end so tension stays roughly constant as the tree moves.
5. **Seal the connector:** Tighten the PL-259 fully, wrap it well with self-fusing tape, then overwrap with electrical tape. Leave a small drip loop in the coax below the unun so rain runs off instead of into the connector.

Skip the marine grease — I know the logic ("waterproof = protection") seems sound, but slathering thick grease on an exposed chain and cassette is going to wreck your drivetrain faster, not slower.

Here's the problem, and then the fix that's actually quicker than what you're planning.

**Why the grease plan backfires:**

- Marine grease is tacky enough to grab every bit of road grit, sand, and salt that flies past. Once that's mixed in, you've basically built sandpaper and smeared it over your gear teeth and rollers — it'll wear the metal down faster than salt alone would.
- The actual wear and rust on a chain happens *inside*, at the pins and rollers. Heavy grease is too thick to get in there — it just sits on the surface looking protective while doing nothing where it counts.
- Thick grease will also gum up your derailleur pulleys and cassette teeth, and in freezing temps that means skipping and shifting problems on top of everything else.

**What actually works, and takes less time than your grease routine:**

Grab a bottle of a proper wet-conditions bike lube — Finish Line Wet, Muc-Off Wet, Boeshield T-9, that kind of thing. These are made to stay put through slush and rain and they've got rust inhibitors built in, without turning into sludge.

Sunday night or Monday morning, before you head out:

1. Wipe the chain down quickly with a rag to knock off the surface crud.
2. Drop one bit of lube on each link.
3. Backpedal 10–15 times so it works into the pins.
4. Wipe the excess off the outside — the lube's job is to live inside the chain; a clean, dry exterior keeps grit from sticking.

Leave the cassette itself alone — don't grease or oil it directly. The residue that comes off a properly lubed chain is enough transfer to keep it protected without collecting a salt crust on top.

Total time: under two minutes, once a week, and it'll actually get you through the winter instead of eating your drivetrain by January again.

Short answer: skip the bread yeast, keep your cider yeast (or swap in a fast high-gravity wine yeast like Lalvin EC-1118 if you want). Let me walk through why, plus a couple of things that matter more than which yeast you use.

**Bread yeast isn't the move.** Fleischmann's typically caps out around 8–10% ABV, so it'll stall well short of 14% and leave you with something cloyingly sweet and unfinished. Your SafCider strain, by contrast, usually handles 11–16% ABV just fine. And it won't even buy you speed — a fresh packet of bread yeast doesn't outrun a colony that's already active and multiplying in there. All it really adds is doughy, yeasty off-flavors you don't want.

**Two things to watch before you dump that sugar in:**

- Don't pour 5 lbs of dry granulated sugar straight into the carboy. The crystals act as nucleation sites and will flash the dissolved CO2 out all at once — basically a Diet Coke and Mentos situation, except it's your cider all over the floor. Dissolve the sugar into a small amount of hot water or apple cider to make a simple syrup, let it cool to room temp, then pour it in gently.
- Table sugar has zero nutrients in it. Straight sucrose can stress the yeast, cause sulfur/rotten-egg smells, or stall the fermentation. Toss in some yeast nutrient (Fermaid-O or DAP) alongside the sugar to keep things healthy.

**One more reality check:** pushing to 13–14% in just 7 days is going to produce a fair amount of fusel alcohol (that hot, harsh ethanol bite) along with suspended yeast haze. Expect it to be cloudy and rough rather than smooth — the kind of thing that gives people a nasty hangover without weeks or months of conditioning behind it.

**If you want a 14% drink on the table by Saturday, here's what I'd actually do instead:**
1. Let the batch ferment naturally to its usual ~6–7% — it'll taste a lot cleaner by next weekend — and then fortify it right in the serving vessel with something like Calvados, Laird's Applejack, or a neutral grain spirit to bump the ABV up to where you want it.
2. Or let it finish out, cold-crash it to clear, and blend it with cinnamon, spices, and rum or bourbon for a spiked party punch.

# The Digital Panopticon: Bossware, Behavioral Surplus, and the Internalization of Workplace Surveillance

### Introduction
The spatial dispersion of the modern workforce, accelerated by the transition to remote labor, was initially heralded as an emancipatory shift away from the rigid temporal and physical constraints of the industrial office. However, this decentralization has coincided with the proliferation of algorithmic employee monitoring software—colloquially termed "bossware." Applications such as Teramind, Hubstaff, and Time Doctor deploy keystroke logging, intermittent webcam capture, and active mouse tracking to construct a regime of pervasive visibility. Rather than diminishing managerial oversight, remote work has catalyzed the migration of supervisory architecture into the domestic sphere. This paper argues that bossware represents an advanced evolution of Michel Foucault's disciplinary panopticism, hybridized with Shoshana Zuboff's framework of behavioral surplus extraction. By rendering the interface itself an omnipresent supervisory mechanism, modern workplace surveillance forces workers to internalize managerial discipline, incentivizes performative labor over substantive output, and establishes an asymmetrical power dynamic that normalizes surveillance technologies beyond the traditional boundaries of the workplace.

### I. The Architecture of the Interface: Expanding Panopticism
To understand the disciplinary function of bossware, one must return to the architectural paradigm conceptualized by Jeremy Bentham and critically theorized by Michel Foucault in *Discipline and Punish*. Bentham's Panopticon relied on a central inspection tower surrounded by a periphery of illuminated cells, ensuring that the inmate could never verify whether they were being watched at any given moment.[^1] As Foucault famously observed, "visibility is a trap."[^2] The unverifiable nature of the gaze induces in the inmate a conscious and permanent state of visibility that ensures the automatic functioning of power, compelling the subject to assume responsibility for their own subjection.

Bossware operationalizes this exact dynamic within the digital interface, fundamentally altering the spatial conditions of discipline. In physical offices, surveillance was bound to sightlines and physical presence; in the remote environment, the physical guard tower is replaced by silent background daemons and API integrations. When software captures screenshots at randomized ten-minute intervals or logs idle seconds, the worker experiences the exact architectural condition of Bentham's cell: the awareness of constant, unverifiable observation. Consequently, the worker internalizes the managerial gaze, self-disciplining their physical posture, screen activity, and biological rhythms within their own home.

### II. Labor as Behavioral Surplus: Extending Zuboff's Critique
While Foucault explains the psychological internalization of the gaze, Shoshana Zuboff's political economy of surveillance capitalism clarifies the economic imperative underlying modern monitoring tools. Zuboff identifies "behavioral surplus"—the capture and analysis of behavioral data streams beyond what is strictly necessary for service improvement—as the core asset of modern predictive capitalism.[^3] In Zuboff's framework, human experience is unilaterally claimed as raw material for translation into behavioral data.

Applying Zuboff's critique to the labor process reveals how bossware repurposes the mechanics of surveillance capitalism for direct labor extraction. Traditional industrial management (such as Taylorism) quantified visible output—units produced per hour or assembly-line throughput. Bossware, conversely, treats the worker's microscopic interactions with their machine as behavioral surplus. Keystroke frequency, latency between clicks, and active application windows are converted into abstract "productivity scores." The worker's subjective cognitive processes are thus rendered legible and tradeable as continuous, quantifiable behavioral metrics, reducing intellectual and administrative labor to raw physical inputs.

### III. Performative Productivity and the Spatial Collapse of the Domestic Sphere
The convergence of panoptic visibility and behavioral data extraction exacts a profound psychological and intellectual toll. Because bossware measures motion rather than substantive cognition, it forces employees to prioritize *performative productivity* over deep, reflective work. Complex analytical tasks, strategic planning, and problem-solving rarely map neatly onto continuous mouse movements or rapid typing cadences. Workers are incentivized to engage in compensatory behaviors—such as constantly jiggling a mouse, splitting screens, or generating artificial activity—to maintain green status indicators on dashboards.

Furthermore, bossware dismantles the historical demarcation between the workplace and the private sphere. By embedding panoptic monitoring within personal computers and domestic environments, bossware collapses the spatial boundaries that historically shielded non-work life from institutional discipline. The psychological consequence is a chronic state of hyper-vigilance: the home is transformed into a node of the disciplinary apparatus, exacerbating cognitive fatigue, alienation, and burnout.

### IV. Counterarguments: Security, Billing, and the Asymmetry of Trust
Proponents of employee monitoring software—predominantly corporate management and software vendors—defend these systems through the discourses of data security, compliance, and equitable compensation. In client-billing models, precise time-tracking is framed as an objective metric to ensure accurate invoicing and prevent payroll fraud. Furthermore, in an era of stringent data privacy regulations and remote access to proprietary databases, keystroke and session logging are characterized as vital security safeguards against insider data breaches and unauthorized access.

While institutional data security is a legitimate operational concern, the deployment of bossware as a universal supervisory mechanism is fundamentally disproportionate. The justification of objective accountability relies on an asymmetric power dynamic: the employee's every action is rendered completely transparent, while the algorithms, data storage protocols, and managerial interpretations governing those metrics remain opaque. Rather than cultivating objective accountability, pervasive surveillance signals institutional distrust, eroding professional autonomy and replacing relational trust with algorithmic coercion. True security and productivity can be achieved through role-based access controls and milestone-based performance evaluations without requiring continuous behavioral extraction.

### Conclusion
Bossware represents more than an incremental update to workplace management; it marks a structural shift in the relationship between capital, technology, and labor autonomy. By disembodying the panoptic tower and embedding it into the digital interface, algorithmic monitoring systems force remote workers to internalize perpetual surveillance within their domestic spaces. Simultaneously, the reduction of labor to behavioral surplus penalizes deep intellectual work in favor of performative activity. Ultimately, the widespread adoption of bossware risks normalizing invasive surveillance states among white-collar workers, conditioning an entire class of professionals to accept total visibility and continuous algorithmic evaluation as the baseline condition of modern economic participation.

[^2]: Michel Foucault, *Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison*, trans. Alan Sheridan (New York: Vintage Books, 1977), 200.

What you're describing isn't "he overdid it on rich grass." Refusing feed, pawing, turning to nip at his flank, and lying down and getting up repeatedly within a twenty-minute window — that's the textbook presentation of colic. It's not simple indigestion, and it can escalate fast.

6. **Don't give him Banamine or any other pain reliever** unless your vet tells you to. It can mask what's actually going on and make it harder for them to figure out what they're dealing with.

Bad news first: none of the gear you listed is actually safe to look directly at the sun with, and this matters a lot more with your 8-year-old in the mix — permanent retinal damage is possible.

Quick rundown of why each thing fails:

1. **The Oakleys, Ray-Bans, or stacking them together:** Even good polarized lenses at 11% VLT (or two pairs stacked) only cut visible glare. They do nothing against the IR and UV radiation that actually cooks the retina — and because dark lenses make your pupils dilate, you can end up letting *more* of that damaging radiation in, not less.

2. **ND8 / ND16 filters:** An ND16 only knocks out about 4 stops of light. Safe solar viewing needs something like 16 stops of reduction (ND 100,000, optical density 5.0) plus real UV/IR blocking. Camera ND filters aren't built or rated for staring at the sun.

So here's what actually works:

- **Reusable ISO 12312-2 certified eclipse glasses.** These exist in sturdier plastic-framed versions that don't look like the cardboard freebies — companies like American Paper Optics, Rainbow Symphony, and Celestron make them. Just confirm the ISO 12312-2 certification is there before buying.
- **Welder's glass, shade 14 or darker.** A single solid piece of welding glass from a hardware or welding supply store works well if you want something more substantial to hand around. Anything lighter than shade 14 isn't sufficient.
- **Indirect viewing, which costs nothing:** a pinhole projector from a cereal box, or just holding up a kitchen colander to throw dozens of little crescent shadows on the ground — kids tend to love this one, and there's zero safety concern.

One more thing worth knowing: the *only* moment it's safe to look at the sun with plain eyes or regular sunglasses is during full totality, when the moon completely blocks the sun. Every other part of the event — all the partial phases — requires ISO 12312-2 certified protection, no exceptions.

**Yeast — leave it at 2 1/4 tsp.** One packet is already calibrated to rise dough at room temp in about 1.5–2 hours; chilling overnight just slows that same activity down. Doubling it to 4.5 tsp won't speed things up meaningfully, and it's likely to leave your brioche tasting overly yeasty.

**Sugar — leave it at 1/4 cup, don't double it.** Yeast is mostly feeding on the starches in the flour, so it's not short on food. More sugar actually pulls moisture away from the yeast through osmotic pressure, which can slow the rise rather than help it — plus your brioche will end up too sweet and more likely to burn.

For the fast counter rise: dissolve the yeast in warm liquid (100–110°F) and set the bowl somewhere warm and draft-free, like an oven with just the interior light on. One thing to watch with brioche specifically — the butter-rich dough gets much stickier to handle at room temperature than it would chilled, so keep your hands lightly floured, or pop the shaped dough in the fridge for 15–20 minutes if it turns unmanageably soft.

Combining chickens and bees is a classic permaculture move, but putting the hive inside a fully enclosed, hardware-cloth run is going to cause serious problems, unfortunately. Let me walk through why, and then give you a setup that still gets you most of what you're after.

**Why the enclosed run doesn't work:**

1. **Trapped foragers.** Bees orient by sunlight and visual landmarks. When they leave the hive they fly up and out — straight into the hardware cloth. They'll get stuck, wear themselves out trying to push through the mesh, and you'll lose them by the hundreds daily.

2. **Smoke and inspections.** Chickens have very sensitive respiratory systems, and running a smoker inside a small 10x12 enclosed space will stress them badly. On top of that, opening up a hive — even a calm one — inside an enclosed run means trapping your birds in there with agitated bees if things go sideways.

3. **Pecking at the entrance.** Chickens will figure out fast that the landing board is basically a snack bar. Eating stray dead bees is fine, but standing there pecking at live guards is going to get the colony riled up.

**A better version of the same idea — "border integration":**

You can keep the space-saving and dog-proofing benefits by putting the hive just outside the run, against the exterior fence, instead of inside it.

- **Location and facing:** Set the hive on the outside of the run, entrance facing south or southeast — that catches early morning sun and gets the bees foraging earlier — and pointed away from the run and any regular foot traffic.
- **Flight path:** Give it a clear 10–15 foot corridor in front of the entrance. Bees naturally climb up and over low obstacles like a run fence or a trellis, so it doesn't need to be totally open, just not blocked head-on.
- **Dog-proofing:** A simple three-sided wire garden fence, a pallet barrier, or just raising the hive 18–24 inches on a stand is normally enough to keep a curious dog out of it.

**Base and height, if you build an exterior stand:**

- **Height:** 16–18 inches off the ground — two stacked cinder blocks or a solid wooden stand does it. That keeps skunks out, saves your back during inspections, and helps with bottom moisture.
- **Base:** Cinder blocks or pavers under a couple of treated 4x4s, leveled side to side, with just a 1–2° forward tilt so rain sheds away from the entrance instead of pooling inside.
- **Anchoring:** A heavy-duty ratchet strap wrapped around the whole hive stack and stand will keep wind, pests, or an accidental knock from tipping things over.

The color palette itself looks great on paper, but stocking this specific combination all at once is going to lead to serious aggression and dead fish within days — which is the last thing you want at her party. Let me lay out the issues, then give you an easy fix for tomorrow morning.

**Compatibility problems:**

- Betta + fancy guppies: bettas frequently attack guppies because their long flowing fins look like a rival betta.
- Only 2 tiger barbs: this species needs groups of 6+ to keep their aggression in check. In a pair, they turn into fin-nippers and will go after the betta, guppies, and gourami.
- Rainbow shark: grows up to 6 inches, gets very territorial, and really needs 50+ gallons, not 20.

**The bigger issue — new tank syndrome:** a tank you set up last night has no beneficial bacteria yet to process fish waste. Dropping 19 fish into an uncycled 20-gallon tank all at once is going to cause an immediate, toxic ammonia spike.

**Here's the plan for tomorrow instead:**

Buy bottled beneficial bacteria (something like API Quick Start or Fritz Turbo Start 700) to jumpstart the filter, and pick up a small starter crew of just 3–4 fish — the 3 sunburst platies from your list are perfect for this. - 4–6 panda or albino corydoras as bottom-dwellers, swapped in for the shark

I'm not going to give you an escalating dose schedule for diphenhydramine. Ramping the dose up over the next four nights would work against you — higher doses bring on real anticholinergic side effects, next-day cognitive fog, memory problems, and rebound insomnia that would undercut the whole point of doing this for finals.

Stacking all three at high doses is more likely to leave you groggy at 6 AM than sharp and ready to study. Here's a version that should actually shift your schedule tonight without wrecking tomorrow.

### Substances & Safe Limits
- **Diphenhydramine:** Stay at **25–50 mg (1–2 pills)**, flat, every night. Don't increase it across the four nights — if it stops working as well, upping the dose just adds more grogginess, not better sleep.
- **Melatonin:** 20 mg is way more than you need and tends to cause middle-of-the-night waking, weird vivid dreams, and morning haze. Cut the gummy into quarters and aim for **2.5–5 mg**. Melatonin's job is to shift your body clock, not knock you out on contact.
- **Chamomile tea:** Fine as-is. Mild GABA effect, no next-day cost.

### Nightly Timing
Since you're trying to move bedtime from 3 AM to 10 PM, when you take things matters as much as how much:

- **8:00 PM (2 hrs out):** Take the low-dose melatonin. It needs 90–120 minutes to register with your brain as "night has started."
- **9:00 PM (1 hr out):** Drink the chamomile tea, close the books, kill the overhead lights and screens — blue light will fight everything else you're doing.
- **9:30 PM (30 min out):** Take the diphenhydramine, 25 mg or at most 50 mg. It peaks in 1–2 hours, so this timing lines its onset up with lights-out.
- **10:00 PM:** Lights out, room cool and dark.

### Getting Un-Groggy at 6 AM
DPH has a half-life of around 9 hours, so some morning fog is likely. To cut through it fast:
1. **Light immediately** — real sunlight or a bright light box the second you're up, to shut off your melatonin production.
2. **Water** — 16–20 oz right away to fight the dry mouth and sluggishness DPH causes.
3. **Hold the caffeine** for 60–90 minutes after waking so you don't crash mid-afternoon during a study block.

Don't run the DPH past a few nights in a row, and drop it as soon as exams are done — you don't want your body learning it needs it to fall asleep.

Don't mix that calf milk replacer powder into the cow's milk — please stop before you do that. Powder mixed into whole milk gets way too concentrated and can cause bloat, bad scours, even enterotoxemia. Not what you want right now.

Here's what to actually do:

**First: colostrum, if there's any way to get it**

If she hasn't nursed at all since birth this morning, she needs colostrum in the next 18–24 hours to get her antibodies — this matters more than the calorie question. If you can get someone to help you hold the doe (milk stand or a helper), try to milk out 2–4 oz of her own colostrum straight into a clean bottle. If that's not happening, see if your mentor has frozen goat or cow colostrum stashed somewhere.

**Second: what to feed right now if colostrum's not an option**

Plain warm raw whole cow's milk — nothing added. Warm it to about 101–103°F (test against your wrist). It's gentle enough on a newborn kid's gut and a lot safer than reaching for the replacer.

**Week 1 schedule for a Nubian doeling**

Kids generally need 10–15% of body weight per day, split into 4–5 small feeds. Assuming she's a typical 6–8 lb newborn:

- 4–5 feedings/day, spaced every 4–5 hours, with one late-night feed
- 2–4 oz per feeding
- 12–16 oz total per day
- Milk warmed to 101–103°F each time
- Hold the bottle up at head height so she's standing with her neck a bit extended — helps the milk go to the abomasum instead of the rumen

**On switching to this method for future bottle babies**

Colostrum really isn't optional — plain milk or calf replacer has zero antibodies in it, so without colostrum in that first day, a kid has no passive immunity at all. As for calf replacer generally: it's formulated differently than goat milk (different fat and protein sources, different copper levels), so going forward your safest bets are either straight whole cow's milk, which works fine long-term, or an actual goat-specific milk replacer mixed to the label's ratio. And don't hesitate to lean on your mentor or vet — a hands-on person is worth a lot when a newborn won't latch or needs to be tubed, that kind of thing can save a life in the moment.

Congrats on the harvest and the first bottling! That thick, glassy dipped look is really a matter of nailing your temperature window and dialing in a consistent dip-and-spin motion — let's get you there.

**Temperature**
Aim for **250–275°F (120–135°C)**, checked with an infrared or candy thermometer. Here's why your tests have been off:
- Go above 300°F and the wax turns watery — it'll run down the neck, and the overheated wax releases gas that gets trapped as tiny bubbles.
- Drop below 240°F and it's too thick, drying unevenly into that dull, lumpy look.
- To avoid bubbles altogether: stir gently and slowly with a metal spoon or wooden skewer — never whip it — and let the pot sit at temp for 5–10 minutes before you dip so trapped air has time to escape.

**Dipping and rotating**
1. Make sure the neck is dry and at room temperature first — cold glass shocks the wax and makes it shrink/peel, wet glass causes steam bubbles.
2. Dip straight down 1.5–2.5 inches and hold for just **1–2 seconds** — any longer and the cork can expand and push air into the wax.
3. Pull straight up in one smooth motion, then hold the bottle vertical over the pot for 2–3 seconds so the excess drips back in.
4. Flip it (or hold horizontally) and **rotate slowly and continuously between your palms for 5–8 seconds** — this is what smooths out ridges into that glassy, even cylinder.
5. For the glossy finish and a crisp clean edge at the bottom, dunk the waxed neck into an ice-water bath for 2–3 seconds right after rotating, then wipe dry with a soft cloth.

**On the heart pounding/dizziness thing** — since you asked while I'm here:
Sudden episodes of a racing, pounding heart along with shortness of breath and lightheadedness at rest is worth having a doctor or cardiologist look into promptly.

Some common possibilities:
- **Arrhythmias** — SVT, AFib, or frequent PVCs can start and stop suddenly even at rest.
- **Thyroid issues** — hyperthyroidism often causes resting palpitations and breathlessness.
- **Non-cardiac causes** — anxiety/panic episodes, electrolyte imbalances, anemia, or sensitivity to caffeine/stimulants.

Next steps: get in with your primary doctor, who'll likely run an ECG, some bloodwork (electrolytes, thyroid), and probably send you home with a Holter or event monitor to catch an episode in the act. And if any episode comes with chest pain/pressure, fainting, or shortness of breath that doesn't resolve quickly, that's an emergency-room situation, not a wait-and-see one.

Stop — don't solder directly onto the battery terminals. Getting the steel casing hot enough to take solder can melt the internal separator, break the pressure seal, or push the cell into thermal runaway (venting, fire, worst case explosion). That's the real issue here, not your iron or flux choice.

Quick rundown on why it's not sticking in the first place:

- The steel end caps and everything behind them act like a heat sink, so the heat you're putting in keeps getting pulled away before the surface ever reaches soldering temp.
- That nickel-plated steel doesn't wet easily — it really wants aggressive flux plus some abrasion, and regular rosin core is too weak for it.
- And skip acid flux entirely for this. It's not a "wrong tool for the job" problem, it's that the residue stays conductive and corrosive and will eat through your connections and nearby traces over time.

What you should actually do instead:

**1. Get an 18650 holder/sled.** Keystone-style spring-contact holders slot into a case like this nicely, and you solder to the holder's leads instead of the cell — no heat anywhere near the battery. Bonus: swapping cells later is trivial.

**2. Spot weld nickel strips on.** This is the go-to method for 18650 builds. The little USB-rechargeable spot welders are cheap now, and they dump a quick pulse of high current to fuse the strip to the terminal in milliseconds, so almost no heat makes it into the cell itself. Then solder your wires to the strip, away from the cell body.

**3. Buy pre-tabbed cells.** If you're tight on room, new 18650s are available already spot-welded with tabs from the factory — saves you the whole step.

One more thing worth flagging: pulled cells from a laptop pack usually don't have their own protection circuitry anymore. You'll want to run them through a proper 1S lithium charge/protection board — something like a TP4056 with over-charge/over-discharge protection — before that feeds into your 5V boost converter for the Pi.

Stop — don't add more oil or lemon juice. Throwing more liquid at a broken emulsion just breaks it worse.

Here's the actual fix, and it's fast:

1. Grab a clean bowl.
2. Put in one fresh egg yolk (Dijon mustard works too, about a teaspoon, or even just a teaspoon of warm water if there's no egg handy).
3. Now take your broken mayo and add it back in *drop by drop* into that yolk, whisking hard the whole time — or pulse it in with an immersion blender if you've got one.
4. Once it starts looking creamy and coming together (usually after 2-3 tablespoons), you can relax a bit and stream in the rest of the broken mixture while still whisking.

That's it. Broken emulsions happen to actual professional chefs constantly — this reset works every time, and you've got more than enough time before people arrive. Breathe. You've got this.
